rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-dhikr, the Reminder, is one of the Quran’s names.
rows.anchor: is one of the names of the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reminder can also mean scripture generally or the Torah; the People of the Book are called the people of the Reminder.
rows.anchor: also employed as a reference to scripture in general or to the Torah

rows.speaker: IK, JJ, Ṭ
rows.claim: They understand the Quran as an honor bestowed on the Prophet and his people.
rows.anchor: the Quran is an honor bestowed upon the Prophet and his people (IK, JJ, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: IK, JJ
rows.claim: The Quran is an honor to them especially because it was revealed in their own language.
rows.anchor: especially since it was a revelation sent down in their own language (IK, JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Because they can best understand its language, the Prophet’s people should be most steadfast in following it.
rows.anchor: they should be the most steadfast in adhering to it (IK)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: They will be questioned in the Hereafter about how fully they fulfilled their duty toward the Quran.
rows.anchor: they will be questioned in the Hereafter regarding the degree to which they have fulfilled their duty toward it (JJ)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The punishment is not lightened even for a single moment.
rows.anchor: for a single moment (IK), since it is inescapable (25:65)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its inescapability means there is no security from the punishment.
rows.anchor: since it is inescapable (25:65), and there is no security from the punishment (70:28)

rows.speaker: Iṣ
rows.claim: Mublisūn conveys regret and being dumbstruck, unable to speak in one’s own defense.
rows.anchor: which also connotes regret and the experience of being dumbstruck, unable to speak in defense of oneself (Iṣ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inhabitants of Hell address Mālik, said to be Hell’s keeper.
rows.anchor: The denizens of Hell will call to the angel Mālik, who is said to be the keeper of Hell

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: They ask to be destroyed so they can gain respite from the Fire’s torments.
rows.anchor: to destroy them, so that they will receive some respite from the torments of the Fire (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their wish for destruction recalls the disbeliever’s wish on Judgment Day to be dust.
rows.anchor: Similarly, on the Day of Judgment, the disbeliever says, “Oh, would that I were dust!” (78:40)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request also recalls those cast in a narrow place who call to be destroyed.
rows.anchor: when they are cast bound together into a narrow place thereof, they will, there and then, call to be destroyed (25:13)

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The reply echoes that they cannot die or have punishment lightened, and that this is requital for disbelievers.
rows.anchor: They will not be done away with so as to die; nor will aught of its punishment be lightened for them

rows.speaker: JJ, Q
rows.claim: Mālik’s response is said to take a thousand years; he tells them they will remain there forever.
rows.anchor: Mālik’s response, which is said to take a thousand years (JJ, Q), will be that they are to remain there everlastingly

rows.speaker: Q, R, Z
rows.claim: The reverent experience only worldly physical death and have no death in Paradise.
rows.anchor: The reverent experience only the physical death of this world and experience no death in Paradise (Q, R, Z)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverent are spared afterlife punishment, while disbelievers undergo it continually as if repeatedly dying.
rows.anchor: They will be spared the punishment of the Hereafter, but the disbelievers will experience it continually

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their not tasting death contrasts with the disbelievers’ claim in verse 35 that they will taste only one death.
rows.anchor: that the reverent taste not death stands in contrast to the claim posed by the disbelievers in v. 35

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Protection from Hellfire expresses Divine Mercy, which precedes the Divine Wrath.
rows.anchor: integral to the Mercy of the Divine Nature, which precedes God’s Wrath

rows.speaker: The Prophet
rows.claim: After Companions say a mother would protect her child from fire, the Prophet says God is more tender toward His servants.
rows.anchor: The Prophet then said, “And God is more tender toward His servants than is this woman toward her child.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse recalls the Quran mentioned in verses 2–3.
rows.anchor: This verse harkens back to the reference to the Quran in vv. 2–3

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Its ease upon the Prophet’s tongue partly explains the Quran’s description as a clear Book.
rows.anchor: That itis easy upon thy tongue explains in part how it is a clear Book (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This wording resembles Sūrah 54’s repeated refrain that the Quran is made easy to remember.
rows.anchor: It is similar to the refrain of Sūrah 54: And indeed We have made the Quran easy to remember

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: The Quran’s ease serves its conveyance to others, so they may be admonished and become believers.
rows.anchor: for the purpose of conveying it to others, that they might be admonished and then become believers (JJ)

words: أَرَءَيْتُم مَّا تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is among several challenges for disbelievers to produce evidence verifying their claims.
rows.anchor: This is one of several verses that challenge the disbelievers to bring something to verify their claims

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those invoked apart from God are idols or beings such as jinn whom idolaters treat as partners.
rows.anchor: That which you call upon apart from God means idols or beings such as jinn whom the idolaters treat as partners with God

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The requested book means a revealed scripture.
rows.anchor: Bring me a book is a request that they bring a revealed scripture (Q, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q, R, Ṭ
rows.claim: One interpretation of a vestige of knowledge is a remnant of teachings from earlier people.
rows.anchor: some vestige of knowledge means some remnant from the teachings of those of old (Q, R, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Another interpretation is something written by people before.
rows.anchor: Others interpret vestige of knowledge to mean something that was written by those before (Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: A further interpretation is any authentic report transmitted from earlier sources.
rows.anchor: though it is also understood to mean any authentic report that has been transmitted (R)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Every interpretation asks for evidence establishing the idols’ and jinn’s alleged partnership with God.
rows.anchor: something that indicates the veracity of the idolaters’ claim that these idols and jinn whom they worship are indeed partners with God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Elsewhere the Quran asks whether God gave them a book on whose clear proof they stand.
rows.anchor: or did We give them a book, such that they stand upon a clear proof from it? (35:40; cf. 34:44; 43:21; 68:37–38)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers say this to disparage the Quran’s teaching of bodily resurrection.
rows.anchor: These are the words of the disbelievers when they disparage the Quranic teaching regarding bodily resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage calls people to reflect on nature’s beauty, order, and bounty as signs of Divine Mercy, wisdom, and Resurrection.
rows.anchor: This is one of several passages to call human beings to reflect upon the beauty, proportionality, and bounty of the natural world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sky can refer to the heavens or allude to all creation.
rows.anchor: Here the sky can also mean the heavens or be read as an allusion to all of creation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Creation has no disproportionality; each thing occupies its proper place, as God created the heavens and earth in truth.
rows.anchor: That creation has no rifts means that there is no disproportionality and that each thing is in its proper place

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every delightful kind may refer to everything created.
rows.anchor: Every delightful kind can be taken as a reference to all that is created

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, kulli zawj means every pair, like the Quran’s statement that all things were created in pairs.
rows.anchor: “every pair,” in which case it is similar to 51:49: And of all things We created pairs

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Everything is a reminder of God’s Might and Power and a sign of His Oneness.
rows.anchor: Everything that exists serves as a reminder of God’s Might and Power and an indication of His Oneness (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Penitent servants are those whose hearts turn to God.
rows.anchor: Every penitent servant means all those whose hearts turn to God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The descent of water is connected to the giving of all life; this verse alone calls it blessed water.
rows.anchor: God’s sending down water relates to the giving of all life. Although many verses refer to God’s sending down water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among Quranic references to water being sent down, this is the only one that calls it blessed.
rows.anchor: the present verse provides the only reference to blessed water

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran treats water as the source of all life.
rows.anchor: Water is understood in the Quran as the source of all life, as in 21:30

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other verses warn that God can remove water, and thereby life and blessings, at any time.
rows.anchor: Other verses allude to God’s ability to remove water, thus life and blessings, at any time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because Arabs considered the date palm the best plant, it signifies the highest physical blessings and all fruit and nourishment.
rows.anchor: The date palm was for the Arabs the best of plants. It can thus be understood as a reference to the highest of God’s Blessings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Provision refers to the waters, gardens, grain, and date palms just mentioned.
rows.anchor: As provision for His servants refers to the waters, gardens, grain, and date palms in the previous verses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God revives dead land with the rainwater, as elsewhere stated.
rows.anchor: God revives a dead land with the water that is sent down, as in 16:65

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Coming forth means Resurrection; just as God created the preceding provisions, He will bring forth all humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: The coming forth refers to the Resurrection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revival of earth can also symbolize God reviving spiritually dead hearts.
rows.anchor: the revival of the earth can also be taken as a reference to the manner in which God revives the hearts of those who are spiritually dead

rows.speaker: Bḍ, JJ, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: One interpretation identifies those bearing a burden as clouds carrying moisture.
rows.anchor: A reference to the clouds that carry moisture (Bḍ, JJ, Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies them as pregnant women.
rows.anchor: or to women who are pregnant (Bḍ, Q)

rows.speaker: Bḍ, JJ, Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: One interpretation identifies those coursing easily as ships moving across the ocean’s surface.
rows.anchor: Ships that course upon the surface of the ocean (Bḍ, JJ, Q, Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Bḍ
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies them as planets moving through their stations.
rows.anchor: or the planets that run through their stations (Bḍ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After delivering the message, the Prophet is not accountable for whether disbelievers follow it or for their punishment if they refuse.
rows.anchor: you are not responsible for whether the disbelievers follow it or for the punishment that will afflict them if they do not

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: His continuing responsibility is to remind believers, who benefit from the message.
rows.anchor: you are only responsible to continue reminding the believers who do benefit from the message

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to remind may address believers alone or both believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Remind is aimed at either the believers to the exclusion of the disbelievers or both the believers and the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Reminder here refers to the Quran.
rows.anchor: Here the Reminder is understood as a reference to the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse enjoins Quran preaching, which benefits believers with deeper spiritual insight and greater certainty and knowledge.
rows.anchor: it benefits believers by increasing their spiritual insight

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: One view says Gabriel appeared to the Prophet on the eastern horizon after the Prophet asked to see him in his true form.
rows.anchor: Gabriel appeared to the Prophet on the eastern horizon after the Prophet requested to see him in his true form (JJ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another view says Gabriel appeared in the highest Heaven.
rows.anchor: when Gabriel appeared in the highest Heaven (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation places the Prophet at the horizon during the Night Journey and Ascension.
rows.anchor: when the Prophet reached the horizon during the Night Journey and Ascension

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pagan followers seem to believe in a god and hereafter, but fit them to conjectures and caprices, effectively denying God’s mastery of both worlds.
rows.anchor: by attempting to make this understanding conform to their conjectures and caprices, they in effect deny that God is the Master of this world and the next

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islamic tradition has no agreed definition of grave sins and preserves many different lists.
rows.anchor: there is no agreement on a single definition and there are many different lists of “grave sins”

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Some define grave sins as offenses whose retribution is removed only through repentance.
rows.anchor: Some define grave sins as “sins for which the retribution is not removed except

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Fawāḥish can mean fornication or, more generally, especially atrocious grave sins.
rows.anchor: Indecencies translates fawāḥish, which is often equated with fornication or, more generally, with grave sins that are considered particularly atrocious (Z)

rows.speaker: JJ
rows.claim: Most understand slight sins as minor sins from which one repents.
rows.anchor: Save what is slight is understood by most to mean minor sins from which one repents (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith cited by many commentators says people have a share of fornication through looking, speech, desire, and whether sexual activity occurs.
rows.anchor: The fornication of the eye is by looking, the fornication of the tongue is by talking; the heart wishes and lusts

rows.speaker: Ibn Masʿūd
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd says eyes, lips, hands, and feet commit lesser forms of zina; intercourse makes one a fornicator, otherwise it is slight sin.
rows.anchor: Ibn Masʿūd is reported to have said, “The eyes fornicate by looking, the lips by kissing, the hands by transgressing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even minor sins, though more readily forgiven, should be avoided because of what they may lead to.
rows.anchor: one must still avoid them and be wary of what they may lead to

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: God forgives small sins by keeping one from grave sins and forgives grave sins through repentance.
rows.anchor: Your Lord is of vast forgiveness in that He forgives small sins by keeping one

rows.speaker: al-Baghawī
rows.claim: Al-Baghawī says this phrase may follow praise of the virtuous to keep less virtuous or grave sinners from despairing of God’s Mercy.
rows.anchor: The commentator al-Baghawī says that

rows.speaker: JJ, Q
rows.claim: Being brought forth from the earth refers to God’s creation of Adam from dust.
rows.anchor: Brought you forth from the earth is understood as a reference to God’s creation of Adam from dust (JJ, Q)

words: وَإِذْ أَنتُمْ أَجِنَّةٌۭ فِى بُطُونِ أُمَّهَٰتِكُمْ
rows.speaker: Bḍ, IK, Q
rows.claim: God knows every person before birth, from when humanity was in Adam’s loins.
rows.anchor: the loins of Adam(Bḍ, IK, Q; see 7:172)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since only God knows who is truly pure, people should not congratulate themselves for pious deeds.
rows.anchor: Thus people should not think well of themselves for performing pious deeds

rows.speaker: Z
rows.claim: Pious deeds themselves come only through God’s support.
rows.anchor: the deeds themselves only come through God’s support (Z), as in 4:49

rows.speaker: The Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet warns against crediting companions’ good deeds to them, saying such praise cuts off a companion’s neck.
rows.anchor: The Prophet even enjoined his followers not to ascribe good deeds to their companions, but only to God, saying several times, “Woe to you!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The recommended praise says one thinks a friend has certain qualities, leaves knowledge of him to God, and declares no one pure before God.
rows.anchor: let him say, ‘I think that so-and-so is this and that; God knows best about him, and I would never declare anyone pure before God,’

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This Quranic axiom first occurs here in chronological revelation order.
rows.anchor: This is the first instance of this Quranic axiom in the chronological order of revelation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one is forced to endure punishment accrued through another person’s deeds.
rows.anchor: No one will be forced to endure the punishments accrued through deeds committed by another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A famous hadith says whoever establishes a sinful custom bears its burden and that of everyone following it until Resurrection.
rows.anchor: as in a famous ḥadīth: “Whosoever establishes a sinful custom

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who lead others astray receive double punishment.
rows.anchor: those who lead others astray are said to have “a double punishment”

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The fullest reward is the full reward God has promised people.
rows.anchor: The fullest reward that God has promised to people (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Some interpret the fullest reward as the vision of God.
rows.anchor: according to some, is the vision of God (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The positive refrain follows an ominous refrain: the first stresses wrath for rejecting God and signs, the second mercy through easy access to revelation and truth.
rows.anchor: The first refrain emphasizes the wrath that comes upon those who reject God and His signs, while the second emphasizes the mercy

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Making the Quran easy to remember is mercy: recitation is easy for the tongue, and understanding and memorization for mind and heart.
rows.anchor: its recitation is made easy for the tongue and the understanding and memorization of it are made easy for the mind and heart (Aj)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One hadith praises those who learn the Quran and teach it to others as the best among people.
rows.anchor: The best among you are those who learn the Quran and teach it to others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another hadith says God will never burn in Hell someone who has memorized the Quran.
rows.anchor: If the Quran is enclosed by skin [i.e., memorized by a human being], God will never burn it in Hellfire

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Remember may mean be admonished, and the question may ask who will take admonition or heed.
rows.anchor: could also be understood to mean, “to be admonished” (Aj)

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Either sense can allude to the pretemporal covenant, asking who remembers or heeds the pact with God.
rows.anchor: it can also be understood as a reference to the covenant made between God and human beings before time (see 7:172c)
